About

Hi, I'm Mira.

I write recipes for people who like cooking but don't want to be martyred by it. Mostly vegetables. Sometimes fish. Occasionally a Sunday-long braise, because everyone needs one of those a month.

Brooklyn, NY · Skillet & Stem since 2021

How this started

I cooked the line at a small farm-to-table place in Fort Greene from 2016 through 2020 — a restaurant that closed during the pandemic and is now a coffee shop, which is a very Brooklyn story. I was a sous by the end. I learned to season aggressively, to plate fast, to never trust a clock more than my eyes, and to respect what a vegetable can do if you just let it have its moment in the pan.

When restaurants closed, I started writing down the things I cooked for myself at home — the leftovers, the cleaned-out-the-fridge dinners, the recipes I'd jotted on the back of prep lists. A handful of friends asked for the file. The file became a Google Doc, then a Substack, then this site. Five years later, here we are: 142 recipes, a Sunday newsletter, and a small but very loyal corner of the internet.

"Treat the vegetable like the protein, and the protein like the seasoning."

What "vegetable-forward" actually means here

Not vegetarian. Not even close — I love a roast chicken, a pork shoulder, a piece of crispy fish. But on most plates I cook, the vegetables are doing the heavy lifting and the meat is a flavoring agent, not the headline. Think anchovies in a greens sauté, sausage crumbled into a pot of beans, bacon hiding in the bottom of a braise. The vegetables get the prime real estate; the protein earns its keep.

The recipes here also assume you have a real life. They're written in plain language, they tell you what to look for instead of giving you absolute timings, and they're tested in my actual home kitchen on actual weeknights with actual ingredients from actual Brooklyn grocery stores. If a recipe asks for something obscure, I've either explained where to find it or given you three things to use instead.

My kitchen, my biases

I cook in a 9x11 Brooklyn galley kitchen with one gas burner that runs hot, two that run lukewarm, an oven that's reliably 25°F under what it says, and counter space the size of a cutting board. If a recipe works here, it'll work anywhere. I write with that in mind.

Some honest biases, so we're on the same page:

  • I salt with Diamond Crystal kosher. If you use Morton or table salt, halve the amount.
  • I use European-style butter when it's the star, regular when it's not. Both are fine.
  • Olive oil should be good but doesn't have to be expensive. Trader Joe's California Estate is my house pour.
  • I write in volume and weight where weight matters (bread, pasta dough, anything where 12g of difference changes the outcome).
  • I'd rather you nail the technique than buy the exact ingredient.

No life stories

If there's an essay, it's because it's actually relevant to the cooking. Scroll to the recipe — there's a jump link at the top.

Real timings

The "30 minutes" promise includes prep. If it takes 47 minutes, the recipe says 47 minutes.

Substitutions, named

Every recipe has a substitutions table. I tested the swaps. I'll tell you which are great and which are merely fine.

The Skillet & Stem pantry

If you stock these twelve things, you can make probably 80% of the recipes on this site without a special trip:

Pantry Brand I buy Why
Olive oil Trader Joe's California Estate Peppery, grassy, $11 for a big bottle. House pour.
Kosher salt Diamond Crystal Lighter flake, more forgiving. Always.
Whole peeled tomatoes Bianco DiNapoli or Cento San Marzano Worth the extra two dollars over generic.
Dried chickpeas Rancho Gordo if I'm feeling fancy, Goya if I'm not Both work. The Rancho Gordo are creamier.
Anchovy fillets Ortiz, in olive oil You're not going to taste them. You'll taste their absence.
Soy sauce Pearl River Bridge light soy Cleaner than mass-market. Worth seeking out.
Gochujang & gochugaru Mother-in-Law's The funky, fermented backbone of half my weeknight dinners.
Capers & olives Salt-packed capers, Castelvetrano olives Rinsed capers; pitted olives. Both bring brightness.

A few honest things about this site

There are no ads. There are no sponsored posts. There are no affiliate links pretending to be recommendations. The site is funded entirely by the paid tier of the Sunday newsletter (which is $6/month and which I love you for considering, but which is genuinely optional — the free tier gets every recipe).

I write all the recipes myself. I test each one three times, minimum — once to develop, once to confirm, once to make sure a real human can follow the written instructions without me standing next to them. The food photography is mine too, shot on a Fuji X-T4 next to my one north-facing kitchen window.

If you've made something from the site and want to tell me about it: the comments on each recipe are read, every single one, by me. The Instagram inbox is harder to keep up with, but I try.

Press & previous work

Pieces I've written for other people: Bon Appétit (2023, on Brooklyn farmers markets), Food & Wine (2024, a guide to weeknight braises), Eater NY (occasional), The Counter (2022 long-form on the closure of small restaurants during the pandemic).

Press the site has gotten: The New York Times Sunday food roundup (2024 and 2025), Apartment Therapy's recipe blog list (2024), Saveur's "Sites We Love" (2025).

For press inquiries, brand partnerships I will probably say no to, or to say hello: hello@skilletandstem.test.

"The best way to support the site is to cook from it, leave a comment, and tell one friend. That's the whole funnel. Thank you."

— Mira
